summary: The City Council approved a $150 million, three-year budget to improve public schools, covering infrastructure, technology, green spaces, and curriculum. The note compares the plan with neighboring City A and City B, calling the city's approach more comprehensive. It also covers equity goals, accountability measures such as audits, and plans for alternative revenue.
one_line: The City Council approved a $150 million, three-year public school improvement budget spanning infrastructure, technology, green spaces and curriculum, with an equity focus.
key_facts: As of September 15, 2023, the City Council, led by Council Chairperson Amanda Richardson and endorsed by Mayor James O'Connor, approved funds for public school improvements.
The total approved budget is $150 million, distributed over three years.
Nearly $60 million goes to physical improvements of school buildings, including modern safety standards, accessibility for students with disabilities, and sports facilities and auditoriums.
Public Works Commissioner Helen Gustafson said outdated HVAC systems will be replaced for better air quality and comfort.

Around $30 million is for classroom technology such as smart boards, educational software, and high-speed internet; Chief Technology Officer Sarah Mendez framed it as bridging the digital divide for lower-income students.
$10 million is allotted for green spaces in school compounds; environmental psychologist Dr. Emily Nguyen suggests nature exposure helps children's cognitive growth and reduces stress.
$25 million is set aside for curriculum development to promote critical thinking and problem-solving beyond rote learning.
Neighboring City A approved a $100 million school budget prioritizing technology over infrastructure.
City B emphasized teacher training without significantly increasing its budget for school facilities or resources.
Equity advisor Johnathan Li said schools in socioeconomically disadvantaged areas will receive a substantial proportion of the funds.
Finance Director Maria Perez outlined periodic audits and public reporting to avoid cost overruns.
The Council plans alternative revenue through local business partnerships, grant applications, and state-level advocacy for more educational funding.
